In [[category theory]], an abstract branch of [[mathematics]], and in its applications to [[logic]] and [[theoretical computer science]], a '''list object''' is an abstract definition of a [[List (abstract data type)|list]], that is, a [[Finite set|finite]] ordered [[sequence]].

== Formal definition ==

Let '''C''' be a [[Category (mathematics)|category]] with finite [[Product (category theory)|products]] and a [[Initial and terminal objects|terminal object]] 1. 
A '''list object''' over an [[Object (category theory)|object]] {{var|A}} of '''C''' is:
# an object {{var|L}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub>,
# a [[morphism]] {{var|o}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> : 1 → {{var|L}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub>, and 
# a morphism {{var|s}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> : {{var|A}} × {{var|L}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> → {{var|L}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub>
such that for any object {{var|B}} of '''{{var|C}}''' with maps {{var|b}} : 1 → {{var|B}} and {{var|t}} : {{var|A}} × {{var|B}} → {{var|B}}, there exists a unique {{var|f}} : {{var|L}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> → {{var|B}} such that the following diagram [[Commutative diagram|commutes]]:

<div style="margin-left: 2em">[[Image:List object definition.svg|300px|A commutative diagram expressing the equations in the definition of a list object]]</div>

where〈id<sub>{{var|A}}</sub>, {{var|f}}〉denotes the arrow induced by the [[universal property]] of the product when applied to id<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> (the identity on {{var|A}}) and {{var|f}}. The notation {{var|A}}* ([[wiktionary:a la#English|à la]] [[Kleene star]]) is sometimes used to denote lists over {{var|A}}.{{sfn|Johnstone|2002|loc=A2.5.15}}

=== Equivalent definitions ===

In a category with a terminal object 1, binary [[coproduct]]s (denoted by +), and binary products (denoted by ×), a list object over {{var|A}} can be defined as the [[initial algebra]] of the [[endofunctor]] that acts on objects by {{var|X}} ↦ 1 + ({{var|A}} × {{var|X}}) and on arrows by {{var|f}} ↦ [id<sub>1</sub>,〈id<sub>{{var|A}}</sub>, {{var|f}}〉].<ref>[[Philip Wadler]]: [http://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/wadler/papers/free-rectypes/free-rectypes.txt Recursive types for free!] University of Glasgow, July 1998. Draft.</ref>

== Examples ==

* In '''Set''', the [[category of sets]], list objects over a set {{var|A}} are simply finite lists with [[Element (mathematics)|elements]] drawn from {{var|A}}. In this case, {{var|o}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> picks out the empty list and {{var|s}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> corresponds to appending an element to the head of the list.
* In the [[Calculus of constructions|calculus of inductive constructions]] or similar [[Type theory|type theories]] with inductive types (or heuristically, even [[Strong and weak typing|strongly typed]] [[Functional programming|functional]] languages such as [[Haskell (programming language)|Haskell]]), lists are types defined by two constructors, '''nil''' and '''cons''', which correspond to {{var|o}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> and {{var|s}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub>, respectively. The recursion principle for lists guarantees they have the expected universal property.

== Properties ==

Like all constructions defined by a [[universal property]], lists over an object are unique up to [[canonical isomorphism]].

The object {{var|L}}<sub>1</sub> (lists over the terminal object) has the universal property of a [[natural number object]]. In any category with lists, one can define the '''length''' of a list {{var|L}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> to be the unique morphism {{var|l}} : {{var|L}}<sub>{{var|A}}</sub> → {{var|L}}<sub>1</sub> which makes the following diagram commute:{{sfn|Johnstone|2002|p=117}}
